raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a transcatheter strategy to reduce thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation (AF) by excluding the left atrial appendage, the dominant source of thrombus in nonvalvular AF [1]. It is best understood not as a universal substitute for anticoagulation, but as a device-based option for patients with elevated stroke risk in whom long-term oral anticoagulation is unsuitable, unsafe, or not acceptable after shared decision-making [19], [21], [22].

The randomized evidence base began with the Watchman 2.5 device. In PROTECT AF, LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular or unexplained death, but early safety events—especially pericardial effusion—tempered enthusiasm [2]. Subsequent PROTECT AF follow-up and PREVAIL showed an operator-learning curve and improved procedural safety, while confirming broadly comparable stroke prevention versus warfarin [3], [4]. Patient-level and 5-year analyses suggested reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, cardiovascular or unexplained death, and nonprocedural bleeding, with ischemic stroke numerically higher in some analyses [5], [6]. The ASAP study extended feasibility to patients considered ineligible for warfarin, using antiplatelet-based post-implant therapy, but it was nonrandomized [7].

Real-world registries subsequently demonstrated high implant success in older, higher-risk populations. EWOLUTION reported high procedural success and acceptable early safety, with many patients discharged without oral anticoagulation [8], [9]. In the United States, the NCDR LAAO Registry provided a major postapproval evidence platform: early registry data confirmed widespread use in patients with prior bleeding and high thromboembolic risk, while 1-year outcomes showed low ischemic stroke rates but substantial mortality and bleeding reflecting patient frailty and comorbidity [10], [11]. These data underscore that LAAC addresses appendage-related embolism, but not the broader competing risks of death, bleeding, vascular disease, and non-LAA stroke mechanisms.

Device technology has evolved. Watchman FLX was designed to improve conformability, sealing, recapture, and safety; the PINNACLE FLX study showed high procedural success and low serious complication rates [12]. The Amulet occluder, with a lobe-and-disc design, was compared with Watchman in Amulet IDE and was noninferior for safety and effectiveness while achieving more complete LAA sealing, at the cost of more procedure-related complications in some analyses [13]. SWISS-APERO, which incorporated Watchman FLX in part of the comparator arm, similarly highlighted that anatomic sealing differs by device and imaging modality, while clinical event differences remain difficult to prove in modestly sized trials [14].

The direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) era has reframed the question. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients to LAAC versus DOACs and found LAAC noninferior for a composite including stroke, systemic embolism, cardiovascular death, major or nonmajor clinically relevant bleeding, and procedure/device complications [15]. Longer-term PRAGUE-17 follow-up supported durability, but sample size limits precision [16]. OPTION addressed patients after AF ablation and found LAAC reduced nonprocedural bleeding versus continued anticoagulation while preserving noninferiority for death, stroke, or systemic embolism [17]. Conversely, CLOSURE-AF, in a higher-risk population, did not establish noninferiority of LAAC versus best medical therapy, reminding clinicians that benefit is population-dependent and procedure risk matters [18].

Patient selection remains the central determinant of value. Contemporary consensus statements recommend LAAC for nonvalvular AF patients with sufficient stroke risk and an appropriate rationale to avoid long-term anticoagulation, provided life expectancy, bleeding mechanism, anatomy, and procedural risk support intervention [19], [20]. The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline strengthened recommendations for percutaneous LAAO in patients with contraindication to long-term anticoagulation and allows consideration in those with high bleeding risk on anticoagulation [21]. The 2024 ESC guideline remains more cautious, emphasizing anticoagulation as default therapy and individualized decisions when anticoagulation cannot be used [22].

Complications include pericardial effusion/tamponade, device embolization, vascular injury, peridevice leak, and device-related thrombus (DRT). DRT is uncommon but clinically meaningful, associated with increased ischemic events in observational studies and meta-analyses [23], [24]. Pericardial effusion requiring intervention is infrequent in contemporary practice but strongly associated with morbidity and mortality [25]. Imaging with transesophageal echocardiography remains standard for preprocedural thrombus exclusion, intraprocedural guidance, and surveillance; intracardiac echocardiography can avoid general anesthesia in selected centers but requires expertise [26].

Post-implant antithrombotic therapy is unresolved. Early Watchman trials used warfarin plus aspirin, then dual antiplatelet therapy, then aspirin [2], [4]. Registry data show wide variation, with anticoagulation alone often associated with less bleeding than anticoagulation plus aspirin and no clear increase in thrombotic events [27], [30]. Watchman FLX registry analyses suggest dual antiplatelet therapy may be comparable to anticoagulation-based regimens in selected patients [28]. Randomized pilot data from ADALA suggest low-dose DOAC may reduce thrombotic and bleeding events versus dual antiplatelet therapy, but larger trials are needed [29]. Overall, LAAC is a mature but still evolving therapy: its optimal use requires careful patient selection, meticulous implantation, structured imaging follow-up, and individualized antithrombotic management.
